Volcanoes form where molten rock called magma rises through the crust. At
subduction zones an oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate, and water
released from the descending slab lowers the melting point of the mantle
above it. The resulting magma is rich in silica, viscous, and full of
dissolved gas, which is why stratovolcanoes such as Mount Fuji and Mount St.
Helens erupt explosively. Shield volcanoes like Mauna Loa in Hawaii form
over hotspots and erupt runny basaltic lava that flows for many kilometres.
Pyroclastic flows, avalanches of hot ash and gas moving faster than a car,
are the deadliest volcanic hazard. Volcanologists monitor ground deformation
with satellite radar, measure sulfur dioxide emissions, and record swarms of
small earthquakes that often precede an eruption by days or weeks.
